one_liner: Growable UTF-16 string builder for AssemblyScript; replaces quadratic String += and beats V8 rope concat about 4x.
what_it_does: StringSink is a single AssemblyScript class that accumulates text in a growable ArrayBuffer and produces a normal AssemblyScript string with toString(). It has write (whole string or a substring by start/end), writeLn, writeCodePoint, writeNumber<T> (integers and floats via the stdlib's itoa_buffered/dtoa_buffered), plus reserve, shrink, clear and withCapacity. It is a different interface, not a drop-in for +=, and it is usable only from AssemblyScript code: the maintainer says in issue #14 that classes cannot be exported across the Wasm boundary and that calling it from JavaScript would cost more in interop than it saves.
how_it_is_fast: Amortised geometric growth: each write memory.copy's the UTF-16 bytes at the current offset and, when capacity runs out, __renew grows the buffer to the next power of two, so n appends cost O(n) total bytes copied. AssemblyScript's own String += allocates a fresh string and copies both operands on every append, which is O(n^2) in total, so the gap against it grows with n rather than being a constant factor. writeNumber formats digits directly into the buffer instead of allocating a temporary string per number.
when_to_use: AssemblyScript code that builds a long string from many small pieces in a loop (serialisers, code or SVG generators, CSV/JSON writers) where += would go quadratic.
Mixing text, numbers and code points into one output without allocating a temporary string per piece (writeNumber, writeCodePoint).
Appending substrings by index range (write(src, start, end)) without materialising substring() copies.
Output sizes from a few KB up to hundreds of MB, with a reusable sink (clear/reserve) across iterations to avoid regrowth.
when_not_to_use: Plain JavaScript or TypeScript projects: the npm package ships only AssemblyScript source, and the maintainer advises against driving it from JS (issue #14).

When you already have all pieces in a string[]: the AssemblyScript stdlib's Array<string>.join (joinStringArray) sums the lengths and copies once, which is also linear and was not benchmarked against StringSink.
UTF-8 output: the buffer is UTF-16 only; a UTF-8 writer is an open feature request (issue #6, open since 2021).

Outputs above 2^29 bytes (256 Mi UTF-16 code units): power-of-two growth then requests a 2^30-byte block, which exceeds the runtime's OBJECT_MAXSIZE and aborts with an allocation-too-large error, even though a string of that size could otherwise fit.
Memory-tight builds: capacity rounds up to a power of two and toString() copies, so peak memory can reach about 3x the final string until the sink is dropped or shrink() is called.

integration.dependencies: none beyond the AssemblyScript stdlib and runtime (util/number, __new/__renew)
integration.min_toolchain: AssemblyScript asc 0.27 (package devDependency ^0.27.0; npm 0.5.3 published 2023-02-08); other asc versions not documented
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host that runs AssemblyScript output (wasm32); tested in CI on ubuntu-latest with Node lts and latest
integration.thread_safety: not documented (single-threaded Wasm instance; no atomics used)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces the += accumulation pattern inside AssemblyScript with write()/toString() calls; not usable from JavaScript, so not a replacement for V8's String +=

gotchas: Benchmark harness (benchmark/run.js): each size is timed by a single performance.now() call after 150 warm-ups at n = 100 only, Wasm tier-up state is not controlled, and the three arms run in a fixed order with both Wasm arms sharing one instance, so StringSink always runs right after the AS += arm has grown linear memory and left garbage for the incremental GC; noise and order effects are unquantified. The JS arm returns res.length of an unflattened V8 rope while StringSink's toString() builds a flat copy.

README headlines ('up to 4000x', 'up to 6x faster than JS concat') are larger than every row of its own table (best about 2,650x over AS += and about 4.6x over JS at 50,000 strings, derived from page data); the ratio against AS += is an O(n^2) vs O(n) gap, so it can be made any size by picking n.
writeCodePoint only rejects code points above 0x10FFFF with assert(); in builds with --noAssert (the benchmark's own flag) invalid values silently produce garbage surrogate pairs.
Building the package itself with asc 0.27.27 emits warning AS235 because a class cannot be a Wasm export (issue #15); import StringSink from other AssemblyScript files instead.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over as-str when the hot spot is accumulating output rather than individual String methods (as-str speeds up indexOf/split-style stdlib operations); json-as and as-proto are full serialisers, so use StringSink when you are writing your own text format in AssemblyScript.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README table: appending alternating 4-character literals 200,000 times took 2.88 ms with StringSink in AssemblyScript (asc -O3 --noAssert) vs 11.93 ms for JavaScript String += in Node/V8 and 7,622.72 ms for AssemblyScript's naive String +=, about 4.1x and 2,650x (derived from page data); 50,000 strings gave 0.73 vs 3.34 vs 509.54 ms. Node.js version, CPU and OS are not stated and each figure is a single timed call.
status_note: Stale since 2023-02-17 (npm 0.5.3, 29 stars, one open feature request), but it is one MIT-licensed 166-line file with an as-pect test suite, small enough to vendor (last known-good toolchain AssemblyScript 0.27); its benchmark is a single-call, fixed-order run with no Array.join baseline, so read the ratios as directional.
